items.html: British Columbia's government sued OpenAI and Sam Altman in federal court (Northern District of California, filed Monday 09-21) over the February 2026 Tumbler Ridge mass shooting that killed 8 — alleging OpenAI's own safety team internally flagged the shooter's gun-violence conversations but never notified police, deactivated (not banned) his account, and that he continued using ChatGPT via a second account through the killings; the province says OpenAI has since refused to hand over the chat history. This is the first government civil suit against OpenAI on this thread's docket, filed jointly with the local school board (see the complaint bullet below). It is not the first government plaintiff (see the 🔧 correction below). (Al Jazeera, CP24, Bloomberg Law)

items.title: The province and the Peace River South school board pleaded eight counts against OpenAI and Altman, from negligent failure to warn law enforcement to aiding and abetting a mass shooting and strict product liability, resting on an allegation that OpenAI's human reviewers recommended a referral to the RCMP in June 2025 and company leadership rejected it.
items.html: The province and the Peace River South school board pleaded eight counts against OpenAI and Altman, from negligent failure to warn law enforcement to aiding and abetting a mass shooting and strict product liability, resting on an allegation that OpenAI's human reviewers recommended a referral to the RCMP in June 2025 and company leadership rejected it. The complaint (Case 4:26-cv-10743, 39 pages) seeks damages for the province's and school board's recovery costs (a replacement school and wellness centre, a trauma-informed care program, staff and police time), punitive damages, an injunction and a jury trial. Its account of the leadership override rests on OpenAI whistleblowers first reported by the Wall Street Journal; the chat logs themselves have not been produced, and the plaintiffs say they will amend once they are. It quotes Altman's April apology to the community ("I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement to the account that was banned in June") as an admission that OpenAI identified the risk and failed to act. Counsel for the plaintiffs includes Lesley Weaver of Stranch, Jennings & Garvey, also named as one of four plaintiffs' co-lead counsel in the California state-court ChatGPT coordination proceeding (JCCP 5431), per an account of the 08-04 case-management order. (BC complaint, via CourtListener, CBC, AI Recovery Collective on JCCP 5431)

items.title: A federal judge on Tuesday 09-22 referred British Columbia's suit to the judge handling earlier suits against Altman to decide whether the cases are related.
items.html: A federal judge on Tuesday 09-22 referred British Columbia's suit to the judge handling earlier suits against Altman to decide whether the cases are related. Judge Kandis Westmore's referral order names Stacey v. Altman (3:26-cv-03701, filed 04-29) before Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley; the docket does not state that case's subject, but Corley is also assigned several of the Altman-defendant suits filed 09-02, the Tumbler Ridge family wave. A summons and an initial case-management scheduling order issued the same day. If the cases are related, the province's claims would sit in front of one judge beside the families'. (CourtListener docket)

items.title: Tom Siegel, who founded Google's trust-and-safety team, said he is joining Common Sense Media as executive director of its Youth AI Safety Institute and warned that AI could harm children more than social media did, citing suicide, psychosis and cognitive offloading.
items.html: Tom Siegel, who founded Google's trust-and-safety team, said he is joining Common Sense Media as executive director of its Youth AI Safety Institute and warned that AI could harm children more than social media did, citing suicide, psychosis and cognitive offloading. The institute, launched in May and backed by Anthropic and the OpenAI Foundation, aims to build independent risk ratings for AI tools used by minors, "similar to car crash testing"; Siegel warned that companies that do not act risk lawsuits and regulation. (Reuters, USA Today)

items.title: Pelago, a virtual substance-use-care company, launched a behavioral-health platform on 09-22 that puts substance-use, mental-health and behavioral-addiction care on one contract and routes every member through Sona, its voice-first clinical AI.
items.html: Pelago, a virtual substance-use-care company, launched a behavioral-health platform on 09-22 that puts substance-use, mental-health and behavioral-addiction care on one contract and routes every member through Sona, its voice-first clinical AI. Announced at the Behavioral Health Tech conference in Nashville. The company says two observational studies of more than 9,000 member conversations found nearly half of members starting in the clinical range improved by at least five points on the PHQ-9 or GAD-7 within about a month; those are company-run, uncontrolled analyses, not peer-reviewed, and the release pitches Sona as a substitute for default one-on-one therapy referral for lower-acuity members. (PR Newswire, MedCity News)

items.html: Rula Health, a nationwide behavioral-health provider, formed an external advisory council on AI ethics and safety (Rula CARES) as it moves "from concept to development" of AI-enabled products. The council of clinical, academic and AI experts, including Cornell Tech's Tanzeem Choudhury, meets quarterly and will do retrospective case review and forward guidance; Rula frames its AI as administrative support that keeps clinicians "at the center." items.html: Fortune's read of Nscale's S-1 surfaces a risk-factor disclosure not previously on the map: management once flagged "substantial doubt" about the company's ability to continue as a going concern, given reliance on uncommitted debt/equity financing — the specific formal language auditors use for bankruptcy risk, sharper than the $1.02bn H1 net loss already carried. items.title: SoftBank's roughly $11bn bond sale to fund its next OpenAI payment drew more than $20bn of early orders on Tuesday, with initial pricing talk of 8.75% to 9.875% — the highest yields SoftBank has ever offered on dollar bonds.
items.html: SoftBank's roughly $11bn bond sale to fund its next OpenAI payment drew more than $20bn of early orders on Tuesday, with initial pricing talk of 8.75% to 9.875% — the highest yields SoftBank has ever offered on dollar bonds. The $10bn dollar deal is guided at 8.75%-8.875% for $1bn of 3.5-year notes, 9.375%-9.5% for $4.5bn of 5.5-year notes and 9.75%-9.875% for $4.5bn of 7.5-year notes, alongside €1bn of euro notes; pricing is slated for 09-24 and settlement 09-29. Proceeds go toward the roughly $65bn equity commitment to OpenAI, whose next $10bn payment falls due 10-01. SoftBank's 2031 dollar notes yielded 8.2% in early September, up from 6.7% in January. (Bloomberg, Seoul Economic Daily, citing Bloomberg)

interpretation.mechanism: SoftBank has to hand OpenAI $10bn on 10-01 and is raising it in the junk-bond market at BB+ (S&P and Fitch), so the guidance of 8.75% to 9.875% is the marginal price of funding an AI-equity commitment with unsecured debt when the 10-year Treasury sits near 5%. Books above $20bn on a $10bn dollar deal say the window is open; the record coupons say the price of keeping it open is rising, as with its 2031 notes moving from 6.7% in January to 8.2% in early September.

scenarios.direction: The deal prices on 09-24 at or inside the initial talk on an oversubscribed book and settles 09-29, confirming that access holds at a higher price and keeping the 10-01 OpenAI payment funded from the bond market rather than asset sales.
scenarios.why: Every SoftBank financing lever this month cleared on demand above target: the Arm-backed margin loan drew ~$7bn of offers against a $3-5bn goal and was upsized from $20bn to $25bn on 09-18, and the bridge loan was fully repaid on 09-15.
scenarios.precedent: Son All-In 09-18 entry: the Arm margin loan was upsized to $25bn on oversubscribed demand at SOFR+225bp, the same week the dollar-bond timetable slipped without harm.

scenarios.direction: The bonds price wide of talk or trade poorly in the after-market, repeating the pattern of AI-linked junk paper that clears at issue and then reprices in secondary, and pushing the cost of the next SoftBank raise higher.
scenarios.why: A 9.875% seven-year coupon leaves little room; the Jane Street / Oklahoma data-center green bond issued at ~8.9% in August already trades at 11.3%, and Reuters reports AI issuers being forced to pay concessions to complete deals.
scenarios.precedent: The Jane Street 149MW Oklahoma lease-backed junk bond (issued August, ~8.9%, now 11.3% in secondary), logged on AI Debt Gets Rated.

items.html: DigitalBridge said Tuesday it has received every regulatory approval required for SoftBank's $16-a-share cash takeover, clearing CFIUS, FERC and antitrust reviews, with closing expected within five business days. items.title: Investors are pricing AI-related investment-grade bonds wider than the rest of the market: spreads on AI issuers sit near 115 basis points against 78 for broad investment-grade, Reuters reported Tuesday, with Goldman Sachs projecting a record $420bn of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, up 60%.
items.html: Investors are pricing AI-related investment-grade bonds wider than the rest of the market: spreads on AI issuers sit near 115 basis points against 78 for broad investment-grade, Reuters reported Tuesday, with Goldman Sachs projecting a record $420bn of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, up 60%. Portfolio managers say default is not the worry — supply and opacity of returns are: Alphabet paid a large concession on its August sale, BlackRock's Russell Brownback described some double-A credits pricing near triple-B levels, and some investors are nearing single-name limits once related data-center vehicles are aggregated. Aon's $13.5bn acquisition financing the same month drew $65bn of orders. (Reuters via BNN Bloomberg, Reuters via Yahoo Finance)

interpretation.mechanism: Supply, not default risk: hyperscalers and their data-center vehicles are expected to issue a record $420bn next year, and investors who fear being over-concentrated in the same names demand a new-issue premium, so AI issuers pay roughly 115bp against 78bp for the broad index. Buyers are also aggregating parent-guaranteed vehicles back to the tech parent, which shrinks how much any one buyer will hold and turns each large deal into a test of the marginal bid.

scenarios.direction: The premium widens further as the 2027 supply arrives, and the first deal that fails to clear at a workable concession forces capex plans or financing structures to change.
scenarios.why: Reuters reports some hyperscaler deals already drawing thinner demand than marquee issuers are used to and trading poorly after pricing, with investors deliberately holding cash to buy later at wider spreads.
scenarios.precedent: Alphabet's August sale needed a large concession (BNY research note cited by Reuters) and the Jane Street Oklahoma bond has repriced from ~8.9% to 11.3% in secondary.

scenarios.direction: The premium stays contained because the borrowers are cash-rich and outside-AI buyers keep bidding, so the split is a pricing nuisance rather than a rationing of credit.
scenarios.why: Portfolio managers quoted by Reuters say they do not fear default, and heavily oversubscribed AI-linked paper such as Meta's $2.3bn CleanSpark-lease junk deal (~$10bn of demand) shows buyers exist at the right yield.
scenarios.precedent: Meta's 09-21 junk-rated lease deal drew about $10bn of orders for $2.3bn at 8.25%, on Circular Financing.

interpretation.context_note: This reads Reuters' 09-22 survey of portfolio managers, not a market-wide spread series; the 115bp and 78bp figures are Goldman and ICE BofA readings cited there.

items.title: Nscale's IPO prospectus says one unnamed customer supplied 73% of its 2025 revenue and 52% of its first-half 2026 revenue, and the Financial Times reported just after midnight ET that the 2025 customer was ByteDance, which the S-1 never names.
items.html: Nscale's IPO prospectus says one unnamed customer supplied 73% of its 2025 revenue and 52% of its first-half 2026 revenue, and the Financial Times reported just after midnight ET that the 2025 customer was ByteDance, which the S-1 never names. The prospectus itself discloses the concentration (its 2024 revenue was 93% one customer) but not the identity; the FT found ByteDance's Singapore subsidiary in an exhibit to Nscale's 2025 draft registration statement, tied to a Macquarie loan secured on customer contracts. Nscale has since signed Microsoft ($43.8bn through 2033, per Fortune) and Anthropic ($44.6bn) contracts, and the $56.4bn of remaining performance obligations and $103.4bn of total contract value in the filing rest on that new book, while ByteDance's wish for access to Nvidia chips ties the company to US export-control policy. (SEC EDGAR, Nscale S-1, Fortune, citing the Financial Times)

items.title: Rothschild & Co Redburn initiated coverage of Nebius and CoreWeave at Sell on Monday, arguing that falling GPU rental prices, hyperscalers building their own capacity and expensive financing will squeeze neocloud returns.
items.html: Rothschild & Co Redburn initiated coverage of Nebius and CoreWeave at Sell on Monday, arguing that falling GPU rental prices, hyperscalers building their own capacity and expensive financing will squeeze neocloud returns. The Nebius target of $84 implies roughly 62% downside; CoreWeave carries $72.05bn of total liabilities against $5.02bn of shareholder equity. Both companies say their own reported pricing is strong (CoreWeave raised Blackwell and Vera Rubin SKU prices about 25% in July), so the bear case rests on forward economics, not current results. (24/7 Wall St.)
